grade.first_issue: Section 3 makes the unsupported and false central claim that every θ≤90° can eventually be forced. This yields a demonstrably incorrect classification, so Rule A caps the score at 2.
grade.summary: The correct set is θ=180°/n for integers n≥2, not the entire interval (0,90°]. For example, θ=70° is not winning: Shan-Yu may start with angles {35°,35°,110°}. More generally, call an angle marked if it is a positive integer multiple of 70°. This triangle is unmarked, and a direct four-case check shows that every cut of an unmarked triangle has an unmarked child; otherwise the marked angles in the two children would force either 180° or a parent angle to be marked. Shan-Yu can therefore avoid 70° forever. The submission correctly handles θ=90° and gives meaningful reasoning excluding θ>90°, but its claimed strategy for arbitrary θ≤90° is neither constructed nor true.
strengths: The one-step strategy for θ=90° is essentially correct after choosing the two acute angles as the base angles.
The invariant that Shan-Yu can retain a triangle whose angles are all below θ correctly excludes θ>90°, starting for instance from an equilateral triangle.
The angle parametrization of a cut is valid.

errors.description: The final answer includes invalid values such as θ=70°, contradicting the actual discrete classification θ=180°/n.
The assertion that a forced right angle can be manipulated to force every smaller θ is unsupported and false; creating θ in only one child does not control the child Shan-Yu retains.
No necessity argument is supplied to exclude θ≤90° for which 180°/θ is not an integer, and no general strategy is supplied for all actual winning values 180°/n.
